I have been farming this land for 25 years, and I know every corner of my 3.5 mu. At 51, I cannot do the back-breaking work of double-cropping anymore, especially since my husband and some of my children work off-farm and are only home for short spells. That is why I plant spring maize alone—it fits my labor and my well water. I will buy hybrid seed from the county supply shop because I learned long ago that the old traditional seeds cannot match the yield, and the extra cost pays for itself. In late April or early May, after the soil warms, I will hire the rotary tiller to prepare the ground and spread compound fertilizer as a base dressing. When the maize is at the big trumpet stage, I will top-dress with urea. I have a well, but pumping costs electricity and water is tight in Quzhou, so I will irrigate twice at most—once around jointing and once during grain filling if the sky stays dry. I will spray herbicide once after sowing to keep the weeds down, and if armyworms or aphids show up, I will spray insecticide once. I have managed this crop through good years and bad, and if the weather is normal, I expect to harvest about 480 kg per mu.
